questions.q: According to this lesson, what common mistake do platform teams make with observability?
options: They instrument applications carefully but leave the platform's own services — the CI runner, GitOps controller, portal backend — with little more than default logs
They apply distributed tracing to every application but never collect any metrics at all
They only collect metrics once per quarter instead of continuously
They refuse to use logs of any kind and rely entirely on manual testing
questions.explain: The common mistake is treating the platform's own components as mere tooling that doesn't need the same observability rigor as the applications it deploys — even though everything depends on those components staying healthy.

questions.q: Why is the GitOps controller described as one of the most load-bearing production systems in the organization?
options: It is the only component that stores application source code
If it stops syncing, nothing deploys anywhere for any team, because every deployment depends on it
It consumes the most CPU of any service in the cluster
It is the only service that requires a license fee to operate
questions.explain: Because every team's deployments flow through the GitOps controller's reconciliation loop, a failure there stalls delivery for the entire organization at once, not just one team.

questions.q: Which pair of metrics does this lesson specifically recommend tracking on a GitOps controller like ArgoCD or Flux?
options: Number of GitHub stars and total repository size
Developer satisfaction survey score and time-to-first-deploy
Lines of code committed per day and number of open pull requests
Sync latency between a commit and cluster reconciliation, and the reconciliation error rate
questions.explain: The lesson calls out sync latency (time between a Git commit and the cluster reconciling to match it) and reconciliation error rate as core GitOps controller metrics, alongside out-of-sync application count.

questions.q: What makes a service level objective (SLO) on the platform's own services actually useful, according to this lesson?
options: The SLO is reviewed once a year during an annual planning meeting
The SLO is set so loosely that it is never at risk of being breached
Someone gets paged when the SLO is at risk, meaning the platform team carries its own on-call rotation and error budget
The SLO only applies to the applications the platform deploys, never to the platform's own components
questions.explain: An SLO only changes behavior if breaching it triggers a page — which requires the platform team to hold its own on-call rotation and error budget, the same as any other production service owner.

questions.q: In the example trace of a developer clicking "create service" in the portal, why is distributed tracing useful across that request path?
options: It eliminates the need to collect any metrics on the CI runner
It automatically fixes slow hops in the request path without human intervention
It replaces the need for a service catalog entirely
It shows which specific hop — portal backend, service catalog, pipeline trigger, or GitOps commit — is actually slow when the portal feels sluggish
questions.explain: Tracing the full fan-out of a single portal request reveals exactly which component along the path is responsible for added latency, instead of leaving "the portal feels slow" as an unresolved anecdote.
